name: Multi-Region Failover
intent: Survive the loss of a whole region by keeping a copy of the system in another one and moving traffic to it, knowing exactly how much time and data you can afford to lose.
scenario: A shop runs its database and app in region A, with a standby in region B that receives asynchronous replication. Region A becomes unreachable at 25 s. Health checks notice, the standby is promoted, DNS is flipped, and 15 seconds after the promotion region A comes back still believing it is the primary.
problem: A whole region can disappear: a power or network failure, a bad regional deploy, a cloud control-plane outage. Multiple availability zones do not help then. Recovering means detecting the failure, making a copy of the data writable somewhere else and moving every user, and each step costs time and risks data. Two numbers frame the whole decision: RTO (how long you can be down) and RPO (how much recent data you can afford to lose). A bad design can also make things worse: if the old region returns while the new one is accepting writes, two primaries accept conflicting data (split brain).

howItWorks.title: Pick the RTO and RPO you actually need, then the topology
howItWorks.text: RTO is the time to be serving again; RPO is how much recent data you can lose, measured in time. Active-passive keeps a standby that is cold (restore from backups, RTO of hours), pilot light (data replicated, compute off, RTO of tens of minutes), or warm (scaled-down copy running, RTO of minutes). Active-active serves traffic from several regions at once, which cuts RTO to seconds but forces you to solve conflicting writes. Cost grows with every step toward faster recovery.

howItWorks.title: Replicate data across regions: async or sync
howItWorks.text: Asynchronous replication acknowledges the write in the primary region and ships it later, so users see low latency but the standby lags by tens of milliseconds to seconds. Whatever has not arrived when the region dies is lost, and that lost tail is your RPO. Synchronous replication waits for the other region before acknowledging, so RPO is zero, but every write pays the cross-region round trip (often 60 to 150 ms) and writes stall if the link breaks.

howItWorks.title: Detect the failure without crying wolf
howItWorks.text: Health checks probe the region from outside, every few seconds, and declare it dead after N consecutive failures. Detection time is about interval times N: faster checks and a low threshold shrink RTO but trip on a network blip. Checks should come from several vantage points, because one failing checker is not an outage.

howItWorks.title: Promote the standby and fence the old primary
howItWorks.text: Promotion makes the replica writable and starts any compute that was off. It must also bump a fencing token (an epoch number) that the storage layer checks, so a write stamped with the old epoch is rejected. That fence is the only reliable protection against split brain, because you cannot be sure the old region is really dead, only that you cannot reach it.

howItWorks.title: Move the traffic
howItWorks.text: A DNS update or a global load balancer (anycast or health-checked routing) points users at region B. With DNS, clients and resolvers keep the old answer until its TTL expires, and some ignore low TTLs, so the tail of users moves slowly. Global load balancers switch faster because they do not depend on client caches.

howItWorks.title: Fail back deliberately and rehearse it
howItWorks.text: When region A returns, it is stale and possibly diverged. Re-sync it from B (discarding or reconciling any stray writes), make it a replica, and move traffic back in a planned switch. Run game days that really fail a region on a schedule: untested runbooks, expired credentials and undersized standbys only show up when you try.

pros: Survives failures that take out every availability zone in a region
RTO and RPO become explicit numbers you can budget and test
Can also serve compliance needs and put data closer to users when designed for it
Fencing and rehearsed runbooks turn a panic into a procedure
cons: Expensive: a warm or active-active second region roughly doubles infrastructure and data transfer cost
Async replication means a failover can lose acknowledged writes; sync replication slows every write
Complex: replication, DNS, secrets, capacity and config must all exist and match in both regions
Data residency laws may forbid copying personal data to another country, limiting where the standby can be
Rarely exercised code paths rot unless you rehearse them
whenToUse: The business loss from a regional outage (hours of downtime) exceeds the yearly cost of the second region
Contracts or regulations require stated RTO and RPO targets
Critical systems like payments or healthcare where a region-wide cloud incident is not acceptable
whenNotToUse: Most internal tools and early-stage products: multi-AZ plus tested backups is usually enough, and regional outages are rare
When data residency forbids replicating the data to the other region, unless the standby is in a permitted location
When the team cannot yet run the failover regularly; an untested standby gives false confidence
pitfalls: Trusting a low DNS TTL: resolvers, browsers and mobile apps often cache longer, so some users stay on the dead region
Promoting the standby without fencing the old primary, so a returning region accepts writes and the two copies diverge
Measuring RPO from an average replication lag instead of the worst case during peak write load
A standby that was never load tested or is missing quotas, secrets, certificates or recent config, so it falls over when traffic arrives
Health checks that run only from inside the failing region, or fail over automatically on a flapping network
Failing back too fast, before the old region has been re-synced, and overwriting newer data
A control plane that is itself in the failed region, so the failover button cannot be pressed

roles.label: Shoppers
roles.description: Browsers and apps that resolve the shop's name and may cache the old address.

roles.label: DNS and health checks
roles.description: Probes the regions and points traffic at a healthy one (DNS record or global load balancer).

roles.label: Primary region
roles.description: Accepts writes and replicates them to the standby.

roles.label: Standby region
roles.description: Holds a replica that can be promoted to primary when the first region is lost.
